about.body1: MYCORE12 maps the preferences that show up in everyday thinking, choices, action, and connection across six paired axes. Each axis contains two positive energies, and both can be useful depending on the situation.
about.body2: Your profile shows the relative balance of all 12 energies and the combination created across six axes. It helps you recognize what comes naturally and practice bringing in complementary energies when they add value.

about.title: What Is MYCORE12?
about.lede: MYCORE12 is a 6-axis preference profile that explores the 12 positive energies reflected in your everyday thinking, choices, actions, and interactions. It describes personality as a pattern of strengths and shows both what comes naturally and where you can broaden your range.
whyBody: People do not approach every situation in the same way. You may move quickly when the direction is clear, then slow down and examine the details when the stakes are higher. In a group, you may naturally align people around a shared plan, or you may do your best work with room to make independent decisions.

MYCORE12 describes these differences through 12 positive energies: Initiative, Deliberation, Coordination, Autonomy, Creativity, Practicality, Analysis, Integration, Empathy, Clarity, Structure, and Flexibility. They form six pairs, and your profile shows the relative balance within each pair.
about.principlesTitle: Three ideas at the center of MYCORE12

principles.title: Every energy has value
principles.body: Initiative creates momentum while Deliberation improves timing and consideration. Empathy reads perspective while Clarity makes expectations and boundaries easier to understand. Each energy can become a strength in the right situation.

principles.title: Scores describe relative preference
principles.body: The two energies on each axis always add up to 100. A 65–35 result means one energy appeared more naturally in your current responses. It does not represent total ability, personal worth, or rank.

principles.title: Growth expands your range
principles.body: You can keep using the strengths that already come naturally while practicing a complementary energy when it would help. MYCORE12 treats growth as adding useful options to the way you respond.

about.resultTitle: What your profile can show you
resultItems: Which energy you tend to reach for more naturally on each of the six axes
The relative balance across all 12 energies
Your current pattern among 64 possible six-axis combinations
How your strengths may show up in work, study, decisions, relationships, and collaboration
Signals to notice when a familiar strength begins to dominate the situation
Practical ways to combine complementary energies
Patterns that may appear under stress and ways to regain balance
about.readTitle: Read the profile name and the scores together
readBody: Your profile name is a memorable headline for the six-axis combination. People with the same profile name can still have different score patterns on individual axes. For a fuller interpretation, read the profile name together with the 12 energy scores and the six paired-axis balances.

An axis close to 50–50 suggests that both energies appeared at similar levels in your responses. A wider gap shows a clearer preference in this assessment. Both patterns provide useful information about how you tend to approach situations.
scopeBody: MYCORE12 is designed for self-understanding, reflection, conversation, and personal development. Individuals can use it to notice recurring preferences, and teams can use shared results as a starting point for discussing differences in working style.
Medical or psychological diagnosis, treatment decisions, hiring, selection, and formal ability evaluation require purpose-built professional methods and evidence appropriate to those decisions.
about.validationBody: The current item set has been developed around the six-axis, 12-energy framework and has completed content review. Sample-based psychometric validation, including reliability and structural testing, is planned as sufficient user data becomes available.

faq.q: Does a higher score mean a better energy?
faq.a: The score shows relative preference within an axis. Both energies can be strengths, and their usefulness depends on the situation.

faq.q: What does a result close to 50–50 mean?
faq.a: It suggests that both energies appeared at similar levels in your responses. You may find that you can move between the two approaches more readily depending on context.

faq.q: Can my result change over time?
faq.a: Some preferences may feel familiar across time, while roles, environments, and recent experiences can influence how you respond. When you retake the assessment, compare the movement on each axis as well as the profile name.

faq.q: What is the difference between 18 and 72 questions?
faq.a: Every length uses the same six axes and 12 energies. Longer versions include a wider set of situations. The 36-question version is the standard format and covers all six contexts evenly.

faq.q: Can I compare my scores with someone else’s?
faq.a: Comparisons are most useful as a conversation about different preferences. In a team, the profile can help people discuss how they communicate, decide, and organize their work.
MYCORE12 is a preference profile for self-understanding and reflection. For medical or psychological diagnosis, use assessment and consultation provided by qualified professionals.

energies.title: The 12 Energies That Shape You
energies.lede: The 12 energies form six complementary pairs. Each pair represents two useful ways of approaching familiar situations. Reading both sides together makes it easier to see what comes naturally and what you can draw on when the context changes.
energies.noteDisclaimer: These notes are general reflections shown to everyone. They are not personalized to your results.

axes.question: How quickly do you turn a decision into action, and how much do you prefer to examine the situation before you begin?

a.name: Initiative
a.definition: Creates a starting point and builds momentum quickly. It is especially useful when the direction is clear and movement matters.
a.useful: starting quickly, moving from decision to action, building early momentum, acting on an opportunity

b.name: Deliberation
b.definition: Examines conditions and possible effects before moving. It helps you improve timing, notice risks, and reduce overlooked details in complex choices.
b.useful: checking risk, setting priorities, making careful choices, considering longer-term effects

axes.together: Initiative gets movement started. Deliberation improves direction and timing. Used together, they help you adjust speed and care to the situation.

axes.question: When working with others, how much do you align the shared flow, and how much do you rely on independent judgment and ownership?

a.name: Coordination
a.definition: Reads shared goals, roles, and pace to create a workable flow across people. It is useful when several contributors need to stay connected and aligned.
a.useful: aligning roles, coordinating schedules, connecting viewpoints, keeping a group focused on a shared goal

b.name: Autonomy
b.definition: Uses independent judgment to carry responsibility forward. It is useful when focused ownership, expertise, and self-directed execution matter.
b.useful: individual ownership, expert judgment, deep focus, independent execution

axes.together: Coordination strengthens the shared flow. Autonomy strengthens individual ownership and expertise. Together, they support collaboration with both connection and initiative.

axes.question: When developing an idea, how much do you explore new possibilities, and how much do you anchor the idea in concrete facts and constraints?

a.name: Creativity
a.definition: Looks for new possibilities, unexpected connections, and alternative directions. It is useful when the path is open and fresh options need to be generated.
a.useful: idea generation, new approaches, early-stage planning, exploring possibilities for change

b.name: Practicality
b.definition: Grounds thinking in observable facts, real conditions, and usable details. It helps turn an idea into something that can be applied in practice.
b.useful: checking feasibility, defining specifications, working through details, building an actionable plan

axes.together: Creativity expands the possibilities. Practicality brings them into contact with reality. Together, they turn new ideas into workable choices.

axes.question: When reaching a conclusion, how much do you separate and compare the parts, and how much do you connect them within the larger context?

a.name: Analysis
a.definition: Breaks a problem into components and compares evidence, criteria, and differences. It is useful for identifying causes, trade-offs, and priorities clearly.
a.useful: diagnosing causes, comparing data, setting criteria, finding errors or inconsistencies

b.name: Integration
b.definition: Connects multiple factors, relationships, and contextual conditions into a coherent whole. It is useful when decisions depend on how several elements interact.
b.useful: seeing the big picture, complex decision-making, balancing stakeholders, connecting multiple sources of information

axes.together: Analysis clarifies the parts. Integration connects the relationships and the whole. Together, they support decisions that account for both evidence and context.

axes.question: In communication, how much do you tune in to another person’s feelings and perspective, and how directly do you express your own expectations and boundaries?

a.name: Empathy
a.definition: Reads feelings and perspective and adjusts tone, timing, and approach accordingly. It is useful when trust and emotional connection matter.
a.useful: listening, emotional support, easing tension, understanding another person’s point of view

b.name: Clarity
b.definition: Expresses thoughts, expectations, requests, and boundaries in direct, understandable terms. It is useful when people need a shared understanding of what comes next.
b.useful: giving feedback, setting expectations, making requests, defining boundaries

axes.together: Empathy pays attention to how a message may be received. Clarity makes the message itself easier to understand. Together, they support communication that is both considerate and clear.

axes.question: When organizing work, how much do you rely on stable standards and routines, and how readily do you adjust the method when conditions change?

a.name: Structure
a.definition: Establishes standards, sequences, and commitments and applies them consistently. It is useful for creating dependable quality and predictable execution.
a.useful: setting standards, managing schedules, maintaining quality, running repeatable work reliably

b.name: Flexibility
b.definition: Adjusts sequence, method, or pace as conditions change. It is useful when unexpected variables or new needs require a quick response.
b.useful: handling surprises, shifting priorities, managing exceptions, adapting quickly

axes.together: Structure creates a dependable baseline. Flexibility adapts the approach to current reality. Together, they support both consistency and responsiveness.

energies.closingTitle: Notice what comes naturally, then widen what is available to you
energies.closingBody: MYCORE12 is designed to keep both energies in view. The goal is to understand the strengths you already use naturally and expand the range of responses you can draw on when another energy would help.

how.title: How MYCORE12 Works
how.lede: Choose the responses that best reflect how you have actually been lately. MYCORE12 turns those choices into a profile showing how naturally you tend to use 12 positive energies across six paired preference axes. You can leave and resume later in the same browser.

steps.title: Read the situation
steps.body: You will see one situation at a time from six contexts: personal life, work and study, relationships, group activities, change and unexpected events, and choices and decisions.

steps.title: Choose the response that feels more natural
steps.body: Read two positive responses and use the five-point scale to show which one is closer to how you have actually been lately. Each response is linked to a different energy on that axis.

steps.title: Review your 12-energy profile
steps.body: See the balance across six energy pairs, all 12 energy scores, your current pattern among 64 combinations, and practical guidance for using your strengths more broadly.

how.axesTitle: What do the six axes measure?
axesItems: Action: Initiative × Deliberation — moving quickly versus taking more time to examine the situation
Collaboration: Coordination × Autonomy — aligning the shared flow versus relying on independent judgment and ownership
Thinking: Creativity × Practicality — exploring possibilities versus grounding ideas in concrete conditions
Judgment: Analysis × Integration — comparing the parts versus connecting the larger context
Relationships: Empathy × Clarity — tuning in to perspective versus expressing expectations directly
Organization: Structure × Flexibility — maintaining consistent standards versus adapting the approach as conditions change
how.scoringIntro: Each question presents two responses linked to different energies on the same axis. The five response positions contribute the following weights:
scoringRows: Much more toward A: A energy 100 / B energy 0
A little more toward A: A energy 75 / B energy 25
A little more toward B: A energy 25 / B energy 75
Much more toward B: A energy 0 / B energy 100
how.scoringBody: Responses across the questions on an axis are combined and normalized for the number of items used. The two energy scores on every axis therefore add up to 100. Across all six axes, the 12 displayed energy scores add up to 600.
how.exampleBody: In this set of responses, Initiative appeared more naturally than Deliberation. The number does not mean that your Initiative ability is “65 out of 100.” It shows relative preference within the Action axis.
how.combinationsTitle: Where do the 64 profiles come from?
combinationsBody: Each of the six axes has two relative preference directions. Combining one direction from each axis creates 2⁶, or 64, possible patterns. The MYCORE12 profile name is a memorable headline for that six-axis combination.

Two people can share the same profile name while having different score gaps on individual axes. The profile name is useful for a quick overview; the 12 energy scores and six axis balances provide the more detailed picture.

lengths.title: 18 Questions — Quick
lengths.body: A concise look at your core tendencies, using three distinct contexts on each axis.

lengths.title: 36 Questions — Standard · Recommended
lengths.body: Each of the six contexts appears once on every axis, giving the standard version an even spread of situations.

lengths.title: 54 Questions — Detailed
lengths.body: Adds more situations on each axis for a more nuanced view of your response pattern.

lengths.title: 72 Questions — In Depth
lengths.body: Covers each axis and context combination more fully, giving you a broader sample of everyday situations.

how.lengthsNote: Every length uses the same six axes, 12 energies, and scoring model. Longer versions simply include a wider range of situations.
how.readingTitle: What to keep in mind when reading your result
readingItems: An axis close to 50–50 is a balanced point where both energies appeared at similar levels
A wider gap shows a clearer preference in this set of responses
Roles, environments, and recent experiences can shift the balance on some axes over time
The scores describe relative preference, not total ability or rank
On a retake, changes in the individual axes often tell you more than the profile name alone
validationBody: The MYCORE12 item set has been developed to represent the six-axis, 12-energy framework through situational questions and has completed content review. Sample-based psychometric validation, including reliability and structural testing, is planned as sufficient user data becomes available.
MYCORE12 is intended for self-understanding and reflection. Medical and psychological diagnosis should be based on assessment and consultation provided by qualified professionals.

guide.title: How to Use Your MYCORE12 Profile
guide.lede: Your profile becomes more useful when you connect it to real situations. Start with the six axis balances, then use the profile name, strength descriptions, and development guidance as layers of the same picture.

steps.title: Start with the six axes
body: Look at the six paired bars before focusing on the profile name. Two or three axes with wider gaps show the areas where preference appeared more clearly in this assessment. Axes closer to 50–50 show places where both energies appeared at similar levels.
items: Which axis has the widest gap?
Which axis is most likely to change with the situation?
Where do I already use both energies at similar levels?

steps.title: Use the profile name as a headline for the whole pattern
body: The profile name is a concise way to remember your six-axis combination. People with the same name can still have different score patterns and experiences, so use the individual axes for the detailed interpretation.

steps.title: Connect your strengths to specific moments
body: Choose two or three statements from “What Comes Naturally to Me” that feel especially accurate and connect them to recent experience.
items: When did this strength help me in the past month?
What do other people tend to rely on me for when I use this strength?
What feels easy to me here that may take more effort for someone else?

steps.title: Use different energies at different stages of work
body: A single task can benefit from different energies as it moves from start to finish.
items: Starting: use Initiative to create movement and Deliberation to check important conditions
Ideas: use Creativity to expand the options and Practicality to define workable constraints
Decisions: use Analysis to compare criteria and Integration to connect the wider impact
Collaboration: use Coordination to align the shared flow and Autonomy to carry ownership forward
Communication: use Empathy to read perspective and Clarity to make expectations and requests explicit
Organization: use Structure to maintain a dependable baseline and Flexibility to adapt when conditions change

steps.title: Use the profile as language for different good approaches in relationships
body: Different energies can make communication easier to understand. One person may prefer a quick decision while another values more time to examine the situation. One person may first attend to feelings and perspective while another naturally makes expectations explicit.
items: This is the approach that feels most natural to me in this situation
What approach works best for you?
How could we combine our strengths through the way we divide roles or sequence the conversation?

steps.title: Practice one complementary energy at a time
body: Choose one behavior that would be useful now rather than trying to change every axis at once. Use the “Using My Strengths More Broadly” and “My Growth Roadmap” sections of your result to select a concrete practice.
items: Choose one situation that comes up regularly
Identify the energy you tend to use first
Choose one complementary energy that would help
Write one specific behavior to try next time
Afterward, note what changed and how it felt

steps.title: Treat stress signals as early cues
body: Under pressure, a familiar strength can become more repetitive or less flexible. Knowing your common signals in advance can help you notice that shift earlier.
items: Am I relying on only one approach more than usual?
Has speed, certainty, independence, or consideration become too dominant for the situation?
Which complementary energy would help restore range right now?

steps.title: On a retake, look for movement on the axes
body: The profile name may stay the same while some axis balances move, or the name may change even though most axes remain similar. Compare where each axis moved, how large the shift was, and whether it connects with changes in your recent role, environment, or experience.

teamBody: Teams can use shared profiles as a starting point for discussing different preferences in meetings, feedback, role ownership, and decision pace. The most useful conversations connect the results to specific working situations.
Role assignment, performance evaluation, hiring, and selection should draw on job-relevant information, observed performance, and professional methods appropriate to the decision.
guide.questionsTitle: Five questions you can use today
questions: Which energy helped me most this week?
Where did one of my familiar strengths stay in the lead for too long?
Which complementary energy might have improved that situation?
Which axis changes the most for me across different contexts?
What is one behavior I can try once in the coming week?
